newsitem.title: GABON: U.S. envoy says peaceful solution possible in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says peaceful solution possible in Zaire.

text.p: South Africa's Vice-President Thabo Mbeki prepared to meet embattled Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko in Gabon on Saturday in a hectic round of diplomacy to negotiate an end to Zaire's civil war.

Speaking earlier in rebel-held Lubumbashi, Mbeki said he had won a commitment from rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose fighters have reached the approaches to the capital Kinshasa, to give diplomacy a chance.
Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said he still believed a peaceful transition in Zaire was possible but that any new government would likely be headed by Kabila.
Mbeki said Kabila had agreed to meet Mobutu on a South African ship on Wednesday for their second round of face-to-face talks and he assumed Mobutu would also agree to attend.
"Mbeki is meeting Mobutu and will put forward the idea of resuming talks with Kabila," said Mbeki's spokesman in Libreville, the Gabonese capital.
Richardson also said a peaceful handover would require another face-to-face meeting between Kabila and Mobutu "probably in the Congo" in the middle of next week.
"I don't think a peaceful transition is dead yet," Richardson said, referring to diplomatic plans formulated by South African officials and U.N. envoy Mohammed Sahnoun.

"A lot of posturing takes place," he said. "I believe that Mobutu will return to Kinshasa before he heads for the Congo. I believe he is putting his affairs in order. But eventually I do believe there's still a good chance of a peaceful inclusive transition government."
Richardson was interviewed on Friday on public television's Newshour with Jim Lehrer shortly after he returned from Paris following shuttle diplomacy throughout Central Africa.
A first ship-borne session between the civil war foes hosted by South Africa's Nelson Mandela ended inconclusively last weekend.
Mobutu's son Nzanga said the president would return to Kinshasa on Saturday after the talks with Mbeki.
"People outside (Zaire) are saying that President Mobutu will go into exile. This is to bring panic. They do not know the president," Mobutu Nzanga told Reuters.

Residents of Kinshasa had speculated that Mobutu would stay away since the rebels were only about 200 km (125 miles) from the city. They fear Mobutu's ragged army may rampage if it forsees inevitable defeat.
No fresh reports of rebel advances have emerged recently and Mbeki said he understood Kabila's military campaign was on hold until after the next talks.
Richardson said Kabila would "most likely" head any transitional government in light of his military victories but that the transitional phase should include various factions.
"The big issue is going to be how much of Mobutu's people, if any at all, are part of that," he said.
Mobutu, 66, dominated the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for more than three decades until prostate cancer and the rebellion, launched in October, loosened his hold.

In Gabon, he met several French-speaking African presidents. They urged Zaire's transition parliament to play a role in ending the war and fill the post of speaker, who would take over in the event of Mobutu's death or incapacity.
France, the most enduring Western backer of Mobutu, a Cold War ally of the United States, welcomed the plan.

But rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha rejected it out of hand, describing the proposal as "absolute nonsense" and saying Mobutu would be chased away if he was still in Kinshasa when rebels arrived.
Karaha demanded that power should be handed directly to "President" Kabila.
In seven months, the rebels, initially a small force fighting for the nationality of ethnic Tutsis, have won control of around three quarters of the vast country.

Giving his impressions of Mobutu, Richardson said the president had not been "facing reality" and had been told by his advisers that "he could still hang on," despite the nearly hopeless military situation throughout the country.
As for Kabila, he said the rebel leader was "very street smart" and pragmatic. But he noted "he's never governed anything -- overwhelmed by the attention and responsibility it takes."

Richardson warned Kabila that he needed to make sure his troops stopped mistreating Rwandan refugees and punished those responsible for refugee massacres in eastern Zaire if he wanted respect from the international community.
"He is going to need private investment and international assistance to survive, because literally Zaire right at this moment is falling apart," Richardson said.
"If he doesn't appear to be handling it in a humane way, he is not going to get help from the international cummunity. In fact he will become a pariah," he added.
